item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles Dodgers prospect Josue De Paula was named Texas League Player of the Year for the 2026 Minor League season. De Paula was among six members of the Drillers organization to receive honors.
Eric Wedge was named Texas League Manager of the Year, while De Paula, Mike Sirota, Zyhir Hope, Jake Gelof and Nick Robertson were all selected to the All-Star team as well. Of course, Hope’s time with the Drillers came to an end at the deadline as he was included in the trade package sent to the Detroit Tigers for Tarik Skubal.
Less than a week after the trade, Hope was named Texas League Player of the Month for July.
Josue De Paula’s Texas League award
De Paula is the fourth Drillers player to be named the Texas League’s MVP, joining Bubba Smith (1996), Ryan Shealy (2004) and Matt Beaty (2017).
The 21-year-old appeared in four games for Tulsa at the end of last season and spent all of this year with the Dodgers’ affiliate before getting called up to make his MLB debut. De Paula became the first Dodgers position player to get promoted directly from Double-A during president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman’s tenure.
While appearing in 124 games for the Drillers, De Paula batted .303/.401/.547 with 37 doubles, two triples, 27 home runs, 104 RBI and 31 stolen bases. He led all Texas League players in total hits (152), RBI and runs scored (106), and was tied for most doubles.
De Paula additionally set career highs in games played, doubles, home runs and RBI. He additionally was one stolen base shy of equaling his most in any Minor League season and three walks shy of tying a career-best mark.
With his RBI and runs scored totals, De Paula joined Carlos Pena as the only players in Drillers franchise history to have at least 100 in both categories in the same season.
De Paula’s impressive offensive success has carried over with the Dodgers, with remarkable plate discipline translating to quality and productive at-bats.
De Paula has garnered praise from Dodgers manager Dave Roberts and teammates alike, and seemingly played his way into the discussion for a potential postseason roster spot. De Paula also has already made Dodgers franchise history as their first player to ever wear No. 95.

The Los Angeles Dodgers called Josue De Paula up from Double-A earlier this month, and he has been making headlines with his bat early on.
It was the first time under Andrew Friedman that the Dodgers called a position player up directly from Double-A. De Paula's defense is not great, but Shohei Ohtani being injured has allowed him to serve as the designated hitter.
In 10 games, he is slashing .286/.474/.500 with half of his hits going for extra bases. His bat and eye at the plate have been as advertised. He is the Dodgers' top prospect and the No. 6 prospect in baseball. He won't be eligible for the postseason since he was not on the 40-man roster by Sept. 1, but his future for the Dodgers looks bright,
He is bound to slump at some point, but his early success means even if he is in Triple-A to start the season next year, it won't be long for him to be back with the big league club. However, Ohtani will be back, and De Paula will need a spot in the outfield. Unfortunately for Teoscar Hernández, he is the most likely to lose his job to De Paula.
Hernández has one year left on his contract, and his OPS has taken a big dive after his All-Star season in 2024. De Paula has shined with the bat and is working hard to improve his defense. If he can do that, he should take Hernández's spot.
What would that mean for Hernández? Well, it's not really the Dodgers' style to trade away their own stars, but De Paula needs to play. Hernández is about to be 34, and he still has trade value. He is not a great defender, so if De Paula is going to replace one of the Dodgers' starting outfielders, it's going to be the one who also isn't great defensively and is old. Kyle Tucker and Andy Pages are not going anywhere.
It's unclear what the Dodgers will do with De Paula next year. They've seen that his bat is ready for the big leagues, but may still want him to get some Triple-A work before making him an every day player in the big leagues. Eventually, he will start to slump in the Majors, like every young hitter, and will have to make adjustments. Regardless, his early success is a threat to Hernández's future with the team.

For the first time under Andrew Friedman, the Dodgers called up a position player directly from Double-A in Josue De Paula.
His bat has been stellar, and even though he is the Dodgers' top prospect and the No. 6 prospect in baseball, defense has been a huge knock on him. He has a 40-grade fielding tool, the lowest of any position player in the top 10 on MLB Pipeline's Top 100 list. The Dodgers even have Jason Heyward, who they hired as a special assistant in the spring, helping him improve defensively.
De Paula knows his defense needs to be better if he wants to make a real impact in the big leagues, and he's not running from it.
"I know that's a big area of improvement for me," De Paula told The Athletic's Fabian Ardaya. "I know I got a lot of hate on it. I'm that type: if I get hate on it, I'm going to focus on it more. So I'm gonna shut a lot of people up with my defense very soon. It's gonna take some time."
So far, De Paula has just one start in the outfield as a big leaguer. However, that's because Shohei Ohtani is currently on the injured list, and the Dodgers have the luxury of playing him in the designated hitter spot. Whether the Dodgers decide to send him back to play in Triple-A or not at some point, he will not be able to serve as a designated hitter permanently.
That spot belongs to Ohtani, so De Paula's path to playing daily is in the outfield. So far, his bat is good enough, and he has great poise at the plate. However, it may actually benefit the Dodgers to have him start next season in Triple-A to iron out his defense.

Josue De Paula has been everything the Los Angeles Dodgers could have hoped for in the batter’s box during since getting called up for his MLB debut.
Since being added onto the Dodgers roster to replace Shohei Ohtani as the everyday designated hitter, De Paula has shown off his patience, ability to take a quality at-bat, and power and speed combination. The sky is the limit for De Paula’s offensive capabilities, and that’s what carried him to the MLB level.
But his defense in the outfield is a major area of concern, and it’s part of the reason the Dodgers did not call De Paula up until needing a regular DH. As they look ahead to the postseason, De Paula is likely to be limited to being a bat off the bench, given his defensive struggles and the uptick of production from Teoscar Hernández and Kyle Tucker.
However, De Paula knows he needs to improve in the outfield, and he’s made it a focus during his first stint at the MLB level.
“Every day. I know that’s a big area of improvement for me, and I know I’ve got a lot of hate on it,” De Paula said. “I’m the type that if I get hate on it, I’m going to focus on it more. I’m going to shut a lot of people up with my defense very soon.”
De Paula has spent time before every game practicing his defense, working with Dodgers coaches to become more of a usable option in the outfield. Dodgers manager Dave Roberts has taken notice of that, and issued a challenge to De Paula.
“Well, it’s clear he needs to improve on his defense,” Roberts said. “How do you shut people up? You perform better. You practice hard, and that’s how you do it. My challenge to him is to be a complete baseball player, and not just to be a hitter. So he’s putting a lot of good work with Dino every day, and so I welcome that.”
Josue De Paula praises Dodgers teammates
De Paula became the first position player promoted from Double-A by Dodgers president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman, creating lofty expectations for himself.
The 21-year-old has felt prepared to meet the challenge of playing in the Majors head-on and credits his Dodgers teammates for creating an environment conducive to letting him play freely.
“Probably the biggest is takeaway is it’s basically the same game, just around different people,” De Paula said on SportsNet LA. “But one thing I didn’t expect was this team to be so cool. Like, all the players, the way they accepted me, the way they greeted me, making me feel comfortable. It put me in a better position to be me.”

item.content:encoded:
With Shohei Ohtani landing on the injured list with knee and biceps issues, the Dodgers called Josue De Paula straight up from Double-A Tulsa to the major leagues.
The move meant he was skipping Triple-A entirely, making him the first position player prospect promoted directly from Double-A under Andrew Friedman's tenure and the first Dodgers hitter to skip Triple-A since Yasiel Puig.
The numbers that got him to the big leagues are absurd. De Paula hit .303 with 27 home runs, 104 RBI, and 29 stolen bases at Double-A this season, an .966 OPS, and MLB had him as the No. 6 overall prospect in the game before the promotion.
An advanced hit tool forcing a September call-up before anyone expected it is exactly what makes a Corey Seager comparison worth investigating. Seager got the call in September 2015, made his debut with a two-hit, two-RBI performance, and then hit .337 with four homers and 17 RBI over his final 27 games of the season. That was enough for the Dodgers to name him the starting shortstop job over veteran Jimmy Rollins heading into October.
Seager and the Dodgers didn't make much noise that year, losing to the New York Mets in the NLDS, but it signaled to the team and fanbase they were willing to give the keys to the kid. Seager wound up leading the Dodgers to the 2017 World Series, and again in 2020, finally winning it all. He was World Series MVP and the NLCS MVP the series before, so LA can only hope this move for De Paula follows somewhat similarly.
Where Josue De Paula fits on the Dodgers' playoff roster
So where does De Paula actually fit for October? With Ohtani out, the DH spot is wide open, and De Paula is expected to see the bulk of his early opportunities there, with some reps in the corner outfield mixed in. Fabian Ardaya of The Athletic mentioned, of his first 37 MLB pitches he has seen that were outside the zone, De Paula has only swung at five, and didn't strike out until his 17th big league at-bat.
If he keeps hitting anywhere close to the way he has in his minor league career and glimpses in these first few games, there's a path to him being a useful bat off the bench or a semi-regular DH option on the postseason roster. That combo would be adding thump, energy and speed the Dodgers don't currently have without sacrificing anything on defense, since he'd be playing a spot that doesn't ask much of his glove yet.
None of that matters unless the Dodgers can legally get him on a postseason roster, and that's going to be a bit of a hurdle. Since De Paula wasn't on the 40-man as of September 1, per MLB's rules regarding postseason roster requirements, the Dodgers need to petition the Commissioner's Office, which requires him to have been in the organization by August 31 and to be replacing an injured player who's already served his minimum IL time.
De Paula clears the first requirement, but the second gets a little trickier. Andy Pages, is one of the options for De Paula to replace, but is also inching closer toward a return around the end of September and likely will be reclaiming his everyday outfield job, not sitting out for procedural reasons.
Dalton Rushing is the more interesting case, since he's already been ruled out from catching this season, and if the front office likes what it's seen from De Paula, shifting Rushing to the 60-day IL cleanly, locks in his unavailability. It opens the exact spot the Dodgers would petition around. In that case, Pages plays center and De Paula takes the roster spot Rushing leaves behind.
It's a real procedural step, not a guarantee, and it depends on the front office actually preferring De Paula's over Rushing. It also assumes the Dodgers have no other injuries before then, which is always a roll of the dice. But if the front office wants De Paula's bat and energy in October, this is the door they'll need to walk through.

The Los Angeles Dodgers' quest to win their third straight World Series title is alive and well, as they have officially clinched the National League West division with eight games left on their schedule. For now, the team's main goal involves getting healthy, but even if it can't, it should still be the favorite to win it all until further notice.
At the trade deadline, the Dodgers did what they always do and went all-in by acquiring the reigning back-to-back American League Cy Young winner, Tarik Skubal, in a trade with the Detroit Tigers. It was almost expected that L.A. would be the team landing Skubal, but according to general manager Andrew Friedman, this was actually a move the team was hoping to avoid having to make.
Andrew Friedman Drops Truth Bomb on Dodgers' Tarik Skubal Trade
With the Tigers failing to sign Skubal to a long-term contract extension over the offseason, he ended up being the big fish that every team wanted at the trade deadline. Of course, landing Skubal was going to require a massive haul of prospects, which is something the Dodgers always seem to have at their disposal.
Los Angeles has developed a reputation for simply being willing to go above and beyond what every other team in the majors is willing to do. Whether it involves shelling out more money for the top free agents, or giving up whatever prospects a team wants for its top player, the Dodgers are always making moves, which is why it wasn't a surprise to see them land Skubal.
Despite that aforementioned narrative continuing to swirl around the team, Los Angeles has claimed that it didn't want to have to make this sort of move this year. According to Friedman, the list of the Dodgers' trade targets started and ended with Skubal, which could help explain why they were so willing to part with several of their top prospects for a guy who is set to hit the free agent market in just a couple of months.
"We looked to do everything we could over the offseason to avoid being a buyer in July, short of a real impact-type talent," Friedman said, per Tom Verducci of Sports Illustrated. "And so, from our standpoint, our buy side list was Tarik Skubal. End of list."
Dodgers' All-In Mindset Could Lead MLB to a Lockout
Trading Skubal was always going to be risky for all 29 other teams in the majors because if he hits the open market, the Dodgers are going to be the favorite to sign him. Without a true salary cap in place, nothing is stopping Los Angeles from spending above and beyond what every other team is spending on its roster, and it has put that theory to the test over the past few years.
It's gotten to the point where a lockout feels inevitable, as the Collective Bargaining Agreement will expire at the conclusion of the season, and there has been virtually no momentum towards a new deal. For now, the Dodgers are intent on winning another championship, but their actions could wind up being at the center of a very important discussion this offseason, with many folks viewing the Skubal trade as the final nail in the coffin.

item.content:encoded:
Shohei Ohtani has taken another step forward in his recovery from right arm and left knee injuries.
On Saturday afternoon, the two-way star did base-running drills on the field during Dodgers batting practice — and began taking simulated at-bats against the team's Trajekt Arc pitching machine behind the scenes in the clubhouse batting cages.
The former was the more visible development, marking the first time Ohtani had been seen on the field performing physical activities since he went on the injured list at the end of last week's homestand.
His work in the hitting cages, however, was a more telling sign of how quickly he might be able to return to action, representing a significant step in what has thus far been a setback-free ramp-up process.
At the start of the week, Ohtani resumed hitting activities with incremental steps. First, he hit off a tee. Then, he took soft tosses from coaches. In recent days, he had begun swinging off a pitching machine, too.
But the Trajekt machine is different; offering players augmented reality at-bats in which a video screen displays a specific pitcher's windup before firing a ball out of a slot from their hand.
In recent years, the technology has become ubiquitous around MLB clubhouses.
And in lieu of a minor-league rehab stint — impossible now with the minor-league season ending — it will be Ohtani's best way to hone a game-ready swing again.
"You hope it bridges the gap a little bit," hitting coach Aaron Bates said. "So between machine, live pitching, Trajekt, somewhere in between that, that's the best you can do."
Bates has been part of the group overseeing Ohtani's recent cage work. He said the slugger has looked "great" and shown no signs of his injuries while returning to full-intensity reps.
"In the cage, in a controlled setting, he's been really good. It's 100% intensity," Bates said. "Once he gets out to the field, if he does a live BP or something like that, and the intensity ramps up, it'll be a good test to see what happens. But in the cage, in the controlled setting, he's been really good."
Before Ohtani went on the injured list, it was evident to the Dodgers' hitting staff that the two-way star "looked extremely compromised," as Bates acknowledged.

One key sign: Ohtani was following through on more of his swings with a one-handed finish, something Bates noted is "always kind of a tell for Shohei, whether he's going through something or not, just because he is disconnected a bit from his back side."
Lately, however, Ohtani's two-handed finish has returned in his swing — as has the Dodgers' optimism that he will be able to provide production in their lineup, despite the 6-for-52 slump he was mired in previously.
"I think everything's been good so far," Bates said.
When Ohtani will be activated remains unclear, with his 15-day stint not up until next Wednesday. But manager Dave Roberts and president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman have said they expect him to be back before the end of the regular season.
Bates echoed that sentiment Saturday, saying Ohtani appears to be "on schedule" while deferring any more specific timeline to the training staff.
Ohtani has not asked to get a specific number of simulated at-bats before being activated, Bates added.
"He just kind of goes how he feels," he said. "And the rehab guys will have kind of the exact quantity kind of laid out for them in that sense."
Time will still tell, of course, whether Ohtani will actually look like himself when he returns, or if he the months he spent playing through his injuries have left him too diminished to make his typical impact with the bat.
As Bates noted, it's possible Ohtani could get a live batting practice session against a pitcher before returning (although the organization is short on arms at the moment capable of doing that, Roberts said Saturday). But beyond that, his Trajekt at-bats will likely account for the bulk of his hitting preparation before returning to game action.
"You kind of fire them out there and see what happens," Bates said. "Just like spring training, it kind of takes guys a little bit of time to get their footing. But it depends on the person. Every guy is a little bit different with how much time they need. Some guys don't need a lot."
Ohtani, Bates said, is in that latter category.
And so far, at least, his hitting progression is going about as well as they could have hoped.

Los Angeles Dodgers president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman is confident Shohei Ohtani will return before the regular season ends.
Friedman told reporters this week that he expects the designated hitter to return before the postseason.
“I expect him back in the regular season,” Friedman declared.
As for how he's doing, Friedman provided a positive update on the superstar.
“He’s doing well,” Friedman said. “He’s progressing well.”
Ohtani is eligible to return from the 15-day injured list on Sept. 23.
That target date leaves Ohtani with only five games remaining until the end of the regular season, and he appears to be on the right track.
“There’s no pain. He’s doing everything he needs to do,” manager Dave Roberts said. “I still don’t know when [the] time to return to play is. But everything that I hear is really positive.”
The 32-year-old is currently sidelined with injuries to his knee, biceps and neck.
Ohtani will focus exclusively on hitting for the rest of the season and into the playoffs after he was shut down from pitching earlier this month, right before he was placed on the IL.
Ohtani was shut down from pitching on Sept. 7, over two months since making his final pitching appearance of the season.
The Dodgers initially placed him on an indefinite pause from pitching on July 19 while he continued to serve as a designated hitter. The hope was he'd be able to return as a pitcher late in the year and into October.
Ohtani was stellar on the mound this season. In 14 appearances, the right-hander went 8-2 with a 1.79 ERA, 95 strikeouts and a 0.95 WHIP in 85.2 innings.
In three seasons as a Dodger, Ohtani has appeared on the mound only 28 times in the regular season.
Shohei Ohtani’s Bat Has Gone Cold Since August
Ohtani's performance was admirable for a few weeks, but since the start of August, his play has declined significantly.
From Aug. 1 until he was placed on the 15-day IL, Ohtani has a .231 batting average with 27 hits, six home runs, 13 RBIs and 19 runs.
Those numbers are far below what Ohtani usually produces at the plate.
Ohtani won't have much time to ramp up for the postseason. It's unlikely the four-time MVP will be back to 100% before October rolls around, but the team is hoping to get anything out of him in the playoffs.

item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles Dodgers rookie Josue De Paula has shown a plate approach and swing that have translated directly to the big leagues. He has cemented himself as a postseason-caliber player.
In his Dodger Stadium debut on September 19th against the San Francisco Giants, De Paula went 2-for-3 with a double, an RBI, and a walk.
It was electric, and hitting in the No. 9 spot, he got on base and scored twice.
Since getting called up, De Paula is hitting .238/.448/.476 in eight games, with eight walks and two strikeouts. His OPS is .924, and while the sample size is limited, the results grow more undeniable game after game.
His production isn’t coming from something high-variance like a high batting average on batted balls; rather, he is delivering through a calculated plate approach, taking walks and never pressing the issue through his 29 plate appearances.
The problem with adding De Paula to the playoff roster
De Paula is “potentially” an option for the postseason roster, according to manager Dave Roberts.
For him to play in October, the team has to jump through hoops. The Dodgers would need to file an exemption with the Commissioner’s Office to add him to the postseason roster.
De Paula was not on the 40-man roster by September 1st, making him technically ineligible unless the Dodgers get the exemption.
They would need a player on the injured list as the reason, making outfielder Andy Pages and catcher Dalton Rushing the two possible postseason casualties.
Given Pages’ status on the team, there is no chance he does not get the nod. Rushing, meanwhile, is trying to swing the bat despite elbow irritation, though he is still a ways from returning.
Something worth noting: Andrew Friedman has a history of letting a hot prospect ride in the postseason.
The Corey Seager Parallel
Seager, at 21, the same age as De Paula, got a call-up on September 3rd, 2015, and he was a sensation from the outset.
He played 27 games and was one of baseball’s best hitters for about a month. Seager slashed .337/.425/.561 with 14 walks, 19 strikeouts, four home runs, and 17 RBIs.
His play earned him a postseason roster spot, where he started. He struggled, hitting .188/.250/.485 with eight strikeouts and 1 walk.
That year, the Dodgers were bounced out by the New York Mets in a five-game thriller. Seager played in all five games.
While Seager struggled, there are reasons to believe that De Paula thrived. He has better discipline and chases less than the young shortstop.
Additionally, De Paula has much more talent and experience around him than Seager did.
With Shohei Ohtani returning, DePaula would be a pinch hitter who is tasked with getting on base. DePaula has success against both left- and right-handed pitching, so that he can be a versatile bat off the bench.
If he keeps performing as he has, Friedman will have another clear decision on his hands — give the young guy a chance to show what he can do.

Like, all the players, the way they accepted me, the way they greeted me, making me feel comfortable. It put me in a better position to be me.”
De Paula is the first position-player Dodgers prospect to be promoted directly from Double-A to the Majors during Andrew Friedman’s tenure as president of baseball operations. Most impressively, he has not looked overwhelmed at the plate despite the jump in competition.
The 21-year-old reached an important milestone last Sunday with the first two hits of his Major League career. The first was a three-run homer. It left De Paula’s bat with a 108.2 mph exit velocity and traveled 416 feet. De Paula flipped his bat in excitement and took a moment to admire the majestic blast.
The reaction from his teammates was an early indication of how open the clubhouse was to the young left-hander.
“It was sick to see all them react that way,” De Paula said. “They were all rooting for me, so they’ve been great and accepted me basically into the team. So it’s awesome.”
Aside from the display of power, De Paula’s plate vision has drawn comparisons to New York Mets slugger Juan Soto. His keen eye was on full display in Monday’s game against the Cincinnati Reds, complete with his own version of the “Soto shuffle.”
While De Paula still has work to do on defense, he has shown the potential to be a foundational building block in the outfield.
Josue De Paula impresses at Dodger Stadium
After beginning his MLB career on the road, De Paula received his first chance to play in front of hometown fans on Friday night and he did not disappoint. He delivered a go-ahead RBI double in the sixth inning and celebrated accordingly upon arriving at second base.
“It felt amazing. To do that for the team, to give us a lead, I’m just celebrating with the boys. I just want to see us win,” he said after the game.
De Paula also reiterated how much he’s been able to learn from teammates and attributed some of his success to the welcoming environment.

Grandes Ligas
Josué De Paula, tres canciones de entrada y un gran doble marcan su memorable debut en el Dodger Stadium
En ocho partidos, el joven dominicano de 21 años suma cinco hits —el primero fue un jonrón de tres carreras contra Eury Pérez de los Marlins—, cinco carreras impulsadas y cuatro anotadas
LOS ÁNGELES.— Josué De Paula dio mucho de qué hablar durante su primera semana en las Grandes Ligas con los Dodgers de Los Ángeles, y eso sin contar el uso de tres canciones de entrada en el mismo partido.
“Fue increíble”, dijo, mostrando una sonrisa deslumbrante.
En su debut en el Dodger Stadium el viernes por la noche, De Paula, que bateó en novena posición como bateador designado, conectó dos hits en tres turnos al bate, anotando dos carreras y produciendo una carrera impulsada. En la victoria por 8-2 sobre los Gigantes de San Francisco, el equipo contrario.
“Tengo muchísima confianza en mí mismo y en mis capacidades”, dijo, “así que sé que cuando llegue el momento, voy a estar a la altura”.
De Paula debutó en las Grandes Ligas el viernes pasado en Miami. En ocho partidos, el joven de 21 años suma cinco hits —el primero fue un jonrón de tres carreras contra Eury Pérez de los Marlins—, cinco carreras impulsadas y cuatro anotadas. Ha recibido ocho bases por bolas y se ha ponchado solo dos veces. Su promedio de bateo es de .238 con un OPS de .924.
“Sabíamos que al llegar a las Grandes Ligas no se iba a sentir abrumado”, dijo el mánager Dave Roberts.
De Paula fue convocado después de que Shohei Ohtani, cuatro veces MVP, entrara en la lista de lesionados y se está ganando un puesto en la plantilla para la postemporada.
“Necesitamos a alguien que salga del banquillo. Él está entre los candidatos”, dijo Roberts. “Sin duda, está haciendo muchas cosas bien”.
De Paula nació y creció en Brooklyn, pero se mudó a la República Dominicana, país natal de su padre, cuando la pandemia de COVID-19 paralizó los deportes en Nueva York, para poder jugar béisbol durante todo el año. Vivió con sus tíos y se matriculó en una academia de béisbol.
Obtuvo la ciudadanía dominicana, lo que le permitió firmar con los Dodgers como agente libre internacional en 2022. Fue ascendido rápidamente a la Clase A al año siguiente, a los 18 años. En 2024, fue ascendido a la Clase A Avanzada.
El año pasado, representó a los Dodgers en el Juego de las Futuras Estrellas , donde conectó un jonrón de tres carreras y obtuvo el premio al Jugador Más Valioso.
De Paula es el primer jugador en ser ascendido directamente desde Doble-A durante los 12 años de Andrew Friedman como presidente de operaciones de béisbol. También es el primer jugador en la historia de los Dodgers en usar el número 95.
Extraoficialmente, podría ser el primer jugador del equipo en usar tres canciones diferentes de entrada al bate en el mismo partido. Como un guiño a sus raíces en Brooklyn —también el distrito neoyorquino donde se originaron los Dodgers— salió al plato en la segunda entrada con la canción "Notorious" de The Notorious BIG, otro nativo de Brooklyn.
“No esperaba que los aficionados me apoyaran tanto, ¡fueron increíbles!”, dijo.
De Paula abrió la quinta entrada con la canción "Ima a Boss" del rapero Meek Mill, en homenaje a su padre, y rápidamente conectó un sencillo para su primer hit en casa. Recibió la pelota y planeaba regalarle el recuerdo a sus padres. Su tercera canción de entrada fue para su madre.
Su doblete con dos outs en la sexta entrada rompió el empate a 2.
“Me encantan sus turnos al bate”, dijo Roberts. “Aprovecha las bases por bolas. Cuando la pelota está en la zona de bateo, puede conectar un jonrón, pero también sabe cómo conseguir un sencillo. Ha sido muy profesional”.
De Paula incluso ganó su desafío utilizando el sistema automatizado de lanzamiento y strike durante un turno al bate.
“Siento la adrenalina, pero creo que sé cómo controlarla y enfocarla”, dijo. “Estoy totalmente concentrado, pero sé cómo tranquilizarme”.
De Paula demuestra un swing sólido y un buen instinto para seleccionar los lanzamientos. En defensa, sabe que necesita mejorar en los jardines.
“Muy pronto voy a callar a mucha gente que se está defendiendo”, dijo.
De Paula ya ha impresionado a su compañero de equipo en los Dodgers y ex Jugador Más Valioso de la Liga Americana, Mookie Betts, quien dijo que era "realmente genial" ver a un jugador joven que puede enfrentarse a cualquier lanzador contrario.
“Le encanta jugar”, dijo Betts. “Cuando está en el campo, se concentra en silencio, pero fuera del campo le gusta bromear y reír. Es un buen chico”.

LOS ANGELES (AP) — Josue De Paula made plenty of noise during his first week in the major leagues with the Los Angeles Dodgers, and that's not even counting his use of three walk-up songs in the same game.
“It was awesome,” he said, flashing a dazzling smile.
Batting ninth as the designated hitter, De Paula went 2 for 3 with two runs and an RBI in his Dodger Stadium debut Friday night, an 8-2 win over the San Francisco Giants.
"I have the utmost confidence in myself and belief,” he said, “so I know when the moment is up for it, I know I’m going to come through.”
De Paula debuted in the major leagues last Friday at Miami. In eight games, the 21-year-old has five hits — his first being a three-run homer off Eury Pérez of the Marlins — five RBIs and four runs. He’s drawn eight walks and struck out just twice. He’s hitting .238 with an OPS of .924.
“We knew that coming up to the big leagues he wasn’t going to get overwhelmed,” manager Dave Roberts said.
De Paula got called up after four-time MVP Shohei Ohtani went on the injured list and is playing his way into a shot at making the postseason roster.
“We need to have somebody coming off the bench. He’s in the mix,” Roberts said. “He’s certainly doing a lot of things well.”
De Paula was born and raised in Brooklyn, but relocated to his father's native Dominican Republic when the COVID-19 pandemic shut down sports in New York so he could play baseball year-round. He lived with his uncles and enrolled in a baseball academy.
He gained Dominican citizenship, which allowed him to sign with the Dodgers as an international free agent in 2022. He was quickly promoted to Class A the following year at age 18. In 2024, he was promoted to High-A.
Last year, he represented the Dodgers in the All-Star Futures Game, hitting a three-run homer and earning MVP honors.
De Paula is the first player to be called up directly from Double-A during Andrew Friedman's 12-year tenure as president of baseball operations. He's also the first player in Dodgers history to wear No. 95.
Unofficially, he may be the first player on the team to use three different walk-up songs in the same game. In a nod to his Brooklyn roots — also the New York borough where the Dodgers originated — he came to the plate in the second inning to “Notorious” by The Notorious B.I.G., another Brooklyn native.
“I didn’t expect the fans to be so supportive and they were awesome,” he said.
De Paula led off the fifth to “Ima a Boss” by rapper Meek Mill in a nod to his father and promptly singled for his first hit at home. He got the ball and planned to give the keepsake to his parents. His third walk-up song was for his mother.
His two-out double in the sixth snapped a 2-all tie.
“I just love his at-bats,” Roberts said. “He takes his walks. When the ball’s in the hitting zone, he can slug you — but he also knows how to get a base hit. It’s been very professional.”
De Paula even won his challenge using the Automated Ball-Strike system during one at-bat.
“I feel the adrenaline, but I just feel like I know how to pinpoint it and focus it,” he said. “I’m so locked in, but I know how to calm myself down.”
De Paula displays a solid swing and an instinct for good pitch selection. Defensively, he knows he needs some work in the outfield.
“I’m going to shut a lot of people up on my defense very soon,” he said.
De Paula has already impressed Dodgers teammate and former AL MVP Mookie Betts, who called it “really neat” to see a young player who can handle any opposing pitcher.
“He loves playing the game,” Betts said. “When he gets on the field, it’s like a quiet focus, but when he’s off the field, he likes joking and laughing. He’s a good kid.”

That's one way to start off the last homestand of the regular season.
Forget the fact that it was against the lowly San Francisco Giants and their lineup featuring a who's who of ... "Who?" Forget the fact that five of the Los Angeles Dodgers' runs in their dominant 8-2 win on Friday night came off the relatively unknown Philip Abner. The Dodgers' lineup, without Shohei Ohtani, showed exactly what they're capable of offensively.
This is the version of the team Andrew Friedman envisioned when he signed Kyle Tucker to a four-year, $240 million contract and Edwin Díaz to a three-year, $69 million deal last winter.
"The talent," manager Dave Roberts said. "It's a high-floor talent level. I just like the way we're taking better team at-bats and making up for not having Shohei in there. Obviously, we're a better team with him, but it is nice to see there hasn't been a drop-off with him not in the lineup."
Here's a look at three winners from the Dodgers' victory over the Giants:
The Dodgers lineup is just fine
Mookie Betts started things off when he jumped on a low-90s fastball that San Francisco starter Cesar Perdomo left middle-middle and sent it over the fence in left center field for his 33rd leadoff home run as a Dodger. The bats went quiet briefly from there until the bottom of the fifth when Teoscar Hernández singled home Josue De Paula from third on a sharp liner to right field to tie the game at 2-2.
The rookie De Paula later drove in the go-ahead run on an RBI double in the sixth before a monster five-run eighth inning in which Max Muncy, Tucker, Betts and Will Smith all went yard to put the game out of reach.
"I think that's the beauty in it," Betts said. "We just keep giving ourselves opportunities and eventually, something will crack. It did tonight, so we just have to keep getting guys on base and giving ourselves the chances and the hits will follow."
Edwin Díaz looked good in return from IL
That set the stage for the trumpets to once again blare over the Dodger Stadium loudspeakers. Roberts said he wouldn't have put Díaz in if it wasn't for the six-run lead as he wanted to give Díaz some leeway in his first outing back from an IL stint after health and poor performance have plagued his season.
But Díaz took the opportunity and ran with it. In his first big league appearance since Aug. 17, he got two quick outs before giving up a base hit up the middle. Rather than let that snowball like it has many times in 2026, however, Díaz was able to buckle down and strike out Brett Harris on three pitches to seal a Dodgers win.
"I liked everything," Roberts said. "I liked his intensity; I liked the fastball velocity. The slider was good. It was just really good to get him back in the mix and that's something to build on."
Josue De Paula is different
The through line for the offense on Friday night was the 21-year-old De Paula. The No. 6 prospect in baseball according to MLB Pipeline finished the night 2-for-3 with a walk, two runs and an RBI, but it was the timing of each of those that made his Dodger Stadium debut so special.
De Paula led off the bottom of the fifth with a base hit, which Betts followed up with one of his own before he eventually scored the tying run on Hernández's RBI single. Two innings later, De Paula scored Tucker from first on a double that he put on a rope at 107 mph deep into the right field gap. As he reached second, De Paula pounded his chest and flexed.
Then, in that huge eighth inning, it was De Paula who kept it alive by working a four-pitch walk with two outs, his seventh in a week in the big leagues. Five pitches later, Betts blew the game open with a two-run homer.
"I just love his at-bats," Roberts said. "It's one of those things that we knew coming up to the big leagues, he wasn't going to get overwhelmed, and it just helps when you control the strike zone. He takes his walks, when the ball is in the hitting zone, he can slug you but he also knows how to get a base hit. It's been very professional."

The Dodgers are the National League West champions.
Again.
They have won their division 13 times in the last 14 seasons, and the one time in that period in which they didn’t, they won a then-club-record 106 games.
Somewhere along the way, the Dodgers did the impossible: They met the requirements to become the sports franchise Los Angeles demanded.
Appreciating what this means requires an understanding of how Shaquille O’Neal and Kobe Bryant transformed this city in the early 2000s,
With O’Neal and Bryant as their stars, the Lakers didn’t just win championships.
They were unbeatable.
This image was reinforced by the play of O’Neal, a 7-foot-1, 325-pound freak of nature who literally couldn’t be stopped.
By the time the Lakers completed their three-peat in 2002, championships were no longer something Los Angeles hoped for.
They became something the city expected.
This is the standard used to measure teams with aspirations of becoming a cultural touchstone in this congested market. With plenty of other entertainment options, casual fans won’t invest too much of their time and money in a team unless they believe it will create the kind of citywide pride O’Neal’s Lakers once did.
The Lakers haven’t been that team for some time. The Rams are producing a worthy on-field product, but they remain in the process of winning back fans they lost over the two decades they spent in St. Louis.
The Dodgers are the one team in town that is clearing the bar.
“What’s funny is Los Angeles has always been looked at, as far as sports, (as) a Laker town,” manager Dave Roberts said. “I think we might have the market share right now in Los Angeles. It’s great. I think we draw more fans than anyone in the world, obviously, with the home dates we have. But it’s 40,000, 50,000 every night. We travel well. I do think the guys see it. They feed off it.”
The Dodgers managed to do this despite playing a sport that is particularly hard to dominate. The Lakers could dump the ball into O’Neal 30 times a game. The Dodgers have employed a number of Hall of Famers over the years, but as great as Shohei Ohtani is, he can only hit four times a game, maybe five.
The Dodgers have become a different kind of juggernaut.
With substantial investment from their owners, they have built some of the deepest rosters in baseball history. In its first season operating the team, Guggenheim Baseball Management signed All-Star outfielder Andre Ethier to an $85 million extension, picked up a then-unknown Yasiel Puig for $42 million, traded for All-Star infielder Hanley Ramirez and assumed more than $260 million in contract obligations in a blockbuster trade for Adrian Gonzalez, Carl Crawford and Josh Beckett.
Season after season, the Dodgers fielded one of the most expensive teams in the major leagues — if not the most expensive team.
Which is why at some point in each of the last 14 seasons, the Dodgers were considered favorites to win the World Series.
They are well into their second decade as baseball’s model franchise — or, depending on the perspective, Evil Empire. The last time they didn’t reach the playoffs, the world was a completely different place. LeBron James had just won his first NBA championship. “Gangnam Style” was a global phenomenon. The recreational use of marijuana was still outlawed in every jurisdiction of the United States.
There’s an entire generation of fans who don’t know what it’s like for the Dodgers to not be legitimate contenders.
Consistency by itself didn’t turn the Dodgers into the Dodgers of today. Actually winning championships was important, of course, and doing that required them to adjust how they built their rosters.
President of baseball operations Andrew Friedman used to operate as if the playoffs were a crapshoot. The organization’s focus was on the regular season, on just reaching the postseason. Because depth is required to survive a 162-game schedule, quantity was emphasized over quality.
The approach didn’t produce any championships. The Dodgers reached the World Series twice in their first eight seasons under Guggenheim ownership but lost both times.
The failures prompted them to pursue real difference-makers.
Mookie Betts, who was the catalyst of the championship team in 2020. Freddie Freeman, the home run hero of the 2024 World Series. Yoshinobu Yamamoto, the Most Valuable Player of the 2025 World Series. And, of course, Ohtani, the franchise’s most transformative player since Fernando Valenzuela, or maybe even Jackie Robinson.
The Dodgers have won three of the last six World Series.
Even with Ohtani dealing with right arm and left knee injuries, they will open the postseason as the odds-on favorites to win their third consecutive championship.
As fragmented as Los Angeles can be, most of the city can get behind that.

Los Angeles Dodgers superstar Shohei Ohtani may play again this season, according to baseball operations president Andrew Friedman.
While taking a ton of champagne and celebrating a 13th National League title in 14 years, Friedman took a question about Ohtani and his outlook.
“He’s doing well,” Friedman said. “He’s progressing well. I expect him back in the regular season.”
Ohtani was not with the team in Cincinnati to celebrate the NL West title; instead, he was in Los Angeles continuing his rehabilitation on his injured right bicep and his left knee.
According to manager Dave Roberts, Ohtani had a day off on Wednesday, though he did hit off a tee and will do some hitting from a coach’s pitches at some point this week.
“There’s no pain. He’s doing everything he needs to do,” Roberts said. “I still don’t know when [the] time to return to play is. But everything that I hear is really positive.”
Does Ohtani need to play in the regular season?
The Dodgers will play Ohtani in the postseason, regardless of whether he plays in the regular season again, general manager Brandon Gomes said, focusing on how he feels rather than his season participation.
“The most important thing is that he’s healthy and in good shape. Whether it’s during the regular season or after that, as long as he’s fully prepared and ready to go, we’re fine with it,” Gomes said, per Japanese reporter Masaya Kotani.
Ohtani has mentioned in the past that he doesn’t get better from playing; rather, rest is the best medicine.
If that is the case and Ohtani can sharpen up a bit with batting practice, sitting him may ensure the Dodgers see the best version of their best player.
Ideally, fans get to see him take some swings over the next week and look better than he did before landing on the injured list.
In his last plate appearances, Ohtani struggled to rotate his body into swings and generate full extension.
He looked to wince after swings, suffering from visible pain in his right arm.
If he can swing fully and tune up his vision for the postseason, it is worth rolling him out, but the Dodgers will err on the side of caution no matter what.

The Los Angeles Dodgers received an encouraging update on Shohei Ohtani as they prepare for the postseason.
Dodgers president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman said Ohtani is "progressing well" after recently resuming light baseball activities. Friedman also said he expects the two-way star to return during the regular season.
Ohtani has been sidelined since the Dodgers placed him on the 15-day injured list with right biceps inflammation and left knee swelling. The move was backdated to Sept. 8, making him eligible to return Sept. 23.
#Dodgers Andrew Friedman said Shohei Ohtani is “progressing well” since starting to swing a bat earlier this week. Ohtani will be eligible to come off IL on Wednesday.
Friedman: “I expect him back in the regular season.”
How many ABs? Friedman shrugged
Ohtani took his first swings off a tee earlier this week without discomfort. The next steps in his progression are expected to include tracking pitches and eventually facing live pitching as he works to regain his timing.
The Dodgers have reason to be cautious with the veteran as they prepare for October. Ohtani has already made 14 starts as a pitcher this season, going 8-2 with a 1.79 ERA and 95 strikeouts in 85.2 innings.
He has also remained a major part of Los Angeles' lineup when healthy. Ohtani is batting .277 with 30 home runs, 80 RBI, 11 stolen bases and a .380 on-base percentage through 130 games.
His absence has come at an important point in the season, but the Dodgers now have some flexibility after clinching the National League West with an 8-2 win over the Cincinnati Reds.
That gives Los Angeles an opportunity to prioritize Ohtani's recovery rather than rushing him back. Friedman did not provide a specific number of at-bats Ohtani will receive before the postseason.
For now, the Dodgers will continue monitoring his progress while gradually increasing his baseball activities. Ohtani's potential return before October gives the club another important storyline to follow during the final days of the regular season.

The NL West continues to run through Los Angeles, as the Dodgers clinched their 13th division title over the last 14 seasons with an 8-2 victory over the Cincinnati Reds on Thursday.
The Dodgers secured their 93rd win— matching their regular season total from last year— thanks in large part to a huge game from Kyle Tucker. Tucker launched his second home run of the four-game set in Cincinnati and collected four hits in five at-bats, finishing just a triple shy of the cycle. For what has undoubtedly been a disappointing first year with his new team, Tucker gave fans a prelude for what they can potentially see from him in October.
Tucker spoke with David Vassegh of SportsNet LA while celebrating their division-clinching win about settling for a double in his final at-bat, noting he wouldn’t have made it safely to third base in his cycle pursuit.
“I tried my best. I don’t think I was going to get there. I probably would’ve been thrown out halfway, but it’s all good.”
Tucker also spoke about the challenges and hurdles he faced repeatedly this season, expressing gratitude for his teammates continuing to stick with him throughout the highs and lows.
“This group is awesome. Everyone supports each other through the ups and downs. We all know where we want to be at the end of the year, and we all just try to help each other out to get there. This is a great group to play with, to play behind, so everyone is super supportive. Everyone knows what we gotta get done.”
With only nine games left for the Dodgers in the regular season, team president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman gave an optimistic update on Shohei Ohtani, noting that they expect him to return from the injured list before their season finale, per Jack Harris of the California Post.
“He’s doing well,” Friedman said, as the team celebrated another National League West title around him at Great American Ball Park. “He’s progressing well.”
“I expect him back in the regular season,” Friedman declared.
Two months ago, Tarik Skubal was still the ace of a Detroit Tigers team on a downward trajectory. On Thursday, Skubal was celebrating the opportunity to pitch in the postseason for a third consecutive season, this time for the reigning two-time World Series champions.
Skubal hopes that the celebrations from Thursday were the first of many more to come as the march for the three-peat is officially in motion, per Maddie Lee of the Los Angeles Times.
“First of many,” he said. “… This is checking a box, and once we get to postseason baseball and doing all that stuff, I think it’s going to be a ton of fun.”
Skubal also reflected on the resiliency of this year’s Dodgers, noting their ability to bounce back after a rough month of August with a current record of 11-5 in the month of September, per Sonja Chen of MLB.com.
“I think there was no panic from this group,” Skubal said. “I think that’s why in big moments, pressure doesn’t really get to these guys.”

CINCINNATI -- Try as they might to view 2026 as its own season, everything the Dodgers have done this year is impossible to separate from the larger context of what they have accomplished in more than a decade of excellence.
The Dodgers hit another key milestone in their title defense by reclaiming the NL West crown with an 8-2 victory over the Reds on Thursday afternoon at Great American Ball Park. Three days after their traditional champagne toast in honor of clinching a postseason berth, winning the West brought on a wild clubhouse celebration -- which they hope will be the first of many over the next several weeks.
"You get so mired in each year, it’s hard to have any perspective," president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman said. "We’ve had our share of troubles this year. Things where we had to work harder than we expected on a couple of fronts. But the important thing is how we finish and how we go into October."
In their record-tying 14 consecutive postseason appearances, the Dodgers have 13 division titles. The only team to unseat them was the 2021 Giants, who edged them in one of the most highly contested NL West races in recent memory.
Since divisional play began in 1969, the Dodgers lead all big league teams with 24 division titles, one more than the Braves -- currently in line to win the NL East -- and three more than the Yankees. Each year's achievements raise the bar for every ensuing year. The expectations facing the Dodgers have become nearly impossible to meet. But they've embraced them gladly.
"There is certainly a higher expectation when, if you don't win the World Series, you fail," manager Dave Roberts said. "But that's kind of part of what you signed up with the Dodgers.”
The Dodgers' offense, whose inconsistency has been a perpetual concern over the course of the season, provided plenty of early support to back a scheduled bullpen game. Kyle Tucker led the way with a four-hit, three-RBI showing, finishing a triple shy of the Dodgers’ first cycle since 2017. Freddie Freeman, Max Muncy, Josue De Paula and Miguel Rojas also knocked in runs.
Justin Wrobleski opened the bullpen game with three perfect innings, and while Blake Treinen surrendered a solo home run in the fourth, Landon Knack pitched four scoreless frames before Seth Halvorsen allowed a run in the ninth.
With nine games remaining in the regular season, the Dodgers are far from full strength. Their best hitter, Shohei Ohtani, is on the 15-day IL, as is first-time All-Star Andy Pages. The six-man rotation they carried for most of the season has been reduced to four fully stretched-out starters on the active roster, necessitating Thursday's bullpen game.
"It's been the same thing the last couple years," Muncy said. "We've had guys go down. We've had guys step up in their place. … That's all that we ask, and we've been able to survive a lot."
The Dodgers are expecting reinforcements back before the postseason, and would greatly benefit from securing a first-round bye to advance directly to the NL Division Series -- giving them five days off after the end of the regular season. They hold a four-game lead over the Braves for the No. 2 seed in the National League.
This edition of the Dodgers is not without its flaws, but then again, neither were the back-to-back champion teams in 2024 and '25. After becoming the first team in a quarter-century to defend their title last year, they will vie for the Majors' first three-peat since the 1998-2000 Yankees.
While the talk of a three-peat began almost from the moment the Dodgers became back-to-back champions last November, Roberts urged his team to stay focused on the present while keeping the larger goal in mind. In his annual speech on the first day of full-squad workouts during Spring Training, he delivered the following message: Be a greyhound, looking forward with blinders on.
Tarik Skubal was not a Dodger when Roberts gave his spring address, but he saw the message play out after he was dealt to L.A. ahead of the Trade Deadline. He arrived at the beginning of a season-high seven-game losing streak -- and the tough stretch gave him a feel for the culture that has led to his new team's sustained success.
"I think there was no panic from this group," Skubal said. "I think that’s why in big moments, pressure doesn't really get to these guys."
The Dodgers have a long road ahead as they look to get back to the World Series, but it bears similarities to the roads they have traveled before. The slate might be wiped clean every year, but they have experience weathering the challenges along the way to the promised land.
"It's a different year, but I think it's kind of the same," Mookie Betts said. "The same group of guys. We know what to expect. We know what to expect from each other. It's the same goal every year. Getting here, you can't really get too focused on how, as long as you get there."

Andrew Friedman, the Los Angeles Dodgers' president of baseball operations, told reporters in Cincinnati that he expects Shohei Ohtani will return during the club's final nine games of the regular season.
Speaking after the champagne celebration that followed the club's 8-2 victory over the Cincinnati Reds that clinched the National League West, Friedman said of Ohtani, "I expect him back in the regular season."
The four-time MVP and two-way superstar will not pitch this season due to right biceps and left knee injuries, and he has not been in the Dodgers lineup since Sept. 7, after which he was placed on the 15-day injured list. Ohtani sat out five games before giving that one a go, and he had just six hits in 49 at-bats (.122) with no home runs in his final 61 plate appearances.
Much of that span was spent trying to also return as a pitcher, before a bullpen session on Aug. 28 was cut short. The club is hoping his focus on playing one side of the ball enables his body not only to heal, but hold up as the Dodgers aim for a third consecutive World Series title.
For the season, Ohtani is batting .277 with 30 home runs and a .902 OPS, and will likely cede his two-year reign as NL MVP to the Chicago Cubs' Pete Crow-Armstrong.

Although the Los Angeles Dodgers are playing without star Shohei Ohtani for the near future, Dodgers president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman thinks it won't be too long before Ohtani is able to make his return.
Ohtani landed on the injured list for the first time in his Dodgers tenure last week, going on the 15-day IL due to right biceps inflammation. But while speaking to reporters Thursday after the Dodgers clinched their fifth straight NL West title, Friedman said Ohtani is on the mend.
"He's doing well," Friedman said, via Jack Harris of the California Post. "He's progressing well."
When asked if Ohtani would be back in time to join the Dodgers in the playoffs, Friedman pointed to the two-way player returning even sooner: "I expect him back in the regular season," he said.
However, Friedman did not provide an answer when asked how many at-bats Ohtani is expected to take, via the Orange County Register's Bill Plunkett.
Because Ohtani's IL stint was backdated to Sept. 8, the earliest he's able to return to the Dodgers' lineup is Sept. 23. Los Angeles will have five games left in the regular season at that point.
Earlier this week, Ohtani took a few hits off a tee in his first swings since going on the IL. Dodgers manager Dave Roberts, like Friedman, said at the time that Ohtani was feeling "good" but that the team planned to give him a "consistent build-up."
Roberts did not have a specific return timetable in mind but, like Friedman, said he was hopeful that Ohtani could return before the postseason.
"Whether it happens or not is to be determined, but I do expect him to be back to play in some regular-season games," Roberts said. "I don't know how many."
With an 8-2 win over the Cincinnati Reds on Thursday, Los Angeles won the NL West for the 13th time in a 14-year span. The Dodgers had clinched a postseason berth earlier this week, marking the team's 14th consecutive year in the playoffs.

CINCINNATI — Amid a champagne-spraying, speaker-blaring, beer-soaked clubhouse scene on Thursday afternoon, there was one matter of on-field business for Dodgers president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman to address.
How was Shohei Ohtani doing in his recovery from right arm and left knee injuries?
“He’s doing well,” Friedman said, as the team celebrated another National League West title around him at Great American Ball Park. “He’s progressing well.”
Well enough for the two-way star — who was rehabbing back in Los Angeles during the club’s division-clinching road trip — to return before the beginning of the playoffs?
“I expect him back in the regular season,” Friedman declared.
Indeed, by all accounts from team officials over the last couple days, Ohtani has been taking encouraging steps forward as he aims to return from the injured list when eligible next Wednesday.
On Tuesday, Ohtani took his first swings since being removed from the active roster, beginning a hitting ramp-up with reps off a batting tee.
And after a day off from activities Wednesday, manager Dave Roberts said before Thursday’s game that the four-time MVP will advance to coach-pitch batting practice later this week.
“There’s no pain. He’s doing everything he needs to do,” Roberts said. “I still don’t know when [the] time to return to play is. But everything that I hear is really positive.”
Roberts described Ohtani as feeling “normal-ish” so far in his recovery work. He noted that the slugger has reported no recurrence of discomfort in his arm as he has begun building back up to a return to the field.
That doesn’t mean Ohtani will get back to 100% in time for October.
The ship on that likely sailed after he tried playing through his injuries, at least as a hitter, during the second half of the season — until it reached the point where he was showing visible signs of pain in multiple games earlier this month.
The Dodgers already know Ohtani won’t be able to pitch in the playoffs, after he endured repeated setbacks in his pitching progression despite not making an actual start since July 3.
They know he might still have to battle through his ailments at the plate in the playoffs, as the team attempts to complete a World Series three-peat.
Still, even having a relatively healthy version of Ohtani could weigh heavily in the team’s championship ambitions.
Not until he returns to action will they know exactly where he is at healthwise, after he suffered a 6-for-52 slump leading up to his IL placement.
But for now, they remain hopeful — of not only having Ohtani back by the start of the playoffs but increasingly likely even before then.

They hit their magic number, but minus the magic.
The Dodgers trudged toward October by clinching their 13th National League West title in 14 years on Thursday, their customary march mired in a quicksand of questions.
Has any Dodger team during this golden era entered the playoffs with more injuries, more uncertainty, and a greater fear of underachievement?
Will the party in Cincinnati be the last time they celebrate this season?
The magic is indeed missing, and after two seasons of conjuring up postseason greatness, these back-to-reality Dodgers appear headed for an early fall.
The Three-Peat looks like a no-go.
Despite the best efforts from baseball’s best braintrust, their latest creation simply doesn’t have the appearance of a championship team.
They’re aging, they’re hurting and, with only a couple of weeks left until the beginning of their annual autumnal angst, they look tired and taut and unprepared for this monumental tussle with history.
“I think for me, the message was, ‘We haven’t come close to playing our best baseball yet.’” manager Dave Roberts told reporters when relaying his speech to the team earlier this week upon clinching a record-tying 14th consecutive playoff berth.
He added, “The message was, we’ve accomplished a lot up to this point, all the while not playing our best baseball. So let’s get some of these guys healthy.”
Haven’t come close to playing our best baseball… Let’s get some of these guys healthy.
Not exactly “Win one for the Gipper” stuff, but completely accurate. These postseason’s themes are more realistic than inspirational, and for good reason.
No, they haven’t come close to playing their best baseball. Forget what you see in these season-ending games against some of the worst teams. Remember, instead, what they’ve done against some of baseball’s best.
Since the All-Star break, they are 4-12 against the five National League playoff contenders. The Atlanta Braves swept them. The Chicago Cubs swept them. The Milwaukee Brewers dominated them.
These teams will be waiting for them in October, and even baseball’s richest roster might not be enough to carry this staggered bunch through their toughest stretch. They’ve played a lot of games in three years, all under baseball’s brightest spotlight, every night, scores of media, millions of fans, a worldwide whirl for 28 regular dudes, and it’s finally taken its toll.
They’ve hit the wall… and the wall is about to hit back.
“It’s not easy, I think it’s a lot harder than people think it is,” said Roberts. “Human nature alone, when you’re hungry, when you’re chasing something, it’s a lot more easy to be motivated, versus, having been there, done that, it gets a little trite, a little old.”
He added: “To keep guys enthusiastic, focused, hungry, that’s harder. But to their credit, they stayed the course. And for me, we’re just as hungry as we were in ‘24 and ‘25. This is a separate season. Our guys understand.”
The 1988-89 Lakers understood, too. And they still got burned in ways that Dodger fans will find painfully familiar. Showtime was chasing the original “three-peat” trademarked by Pat Riley when the Lakers were swept by the Detroit Pistons in a Finals that seemed cursed,
Byron Scott missed the series with a hamstring injury and Magic Johnson essentially missed the final two games with a hamstring injury and they couldn’t survive.
This looks like the Dodgers today. Their injuries feel too major, and the impact too deep.
Start with Shohei Ohtani. The Dodgers haven’t won a full-season championship in 38 years without him at the top of the lineup. He’ll be there again, but his body has been breaking down for the last couple of months, and, before being recently placed on the injured list — finally! — he was only a shadow of himself.
He hasn’t hit a home run or driven in a run outside of Coors Field in more than a month. In his last 24 games before going on the IL with biceps and knee issues, he was batting .198. The Dodgers can’t admit it, and Ohtani would never acknowledge it, but this is a man in serious need of an extended rest.
Teoscar Hernández’s two-run homer Tuesday in the Dodgers’ win against the Reds was his second home run in as many nights.
Also on the injured list in these final days is Andy Pages, who was having a career year before breaking his hand. He’ll return without much time to get ready for October, and this is a man who will need some time, as he has a career .114 average in the postseason and was even benched last year before he redeemed himself with that picturesque catch over Kiké Hernández.
Speaking of last October’s heroes, the biggest savior has also spent the summer in pain, Will Smith battling neck issues until recently returning to the lineup. But the comeback has been bumpy. In his initial games since returning at the start of September, Smith was batting .171. Last October he set a major league record by catching 73 innings in the World Series. He is still paying the price.
Then there’s Freddie Freeman, whose bat doesn’t have the same pop, who’s step doesn’t have the same spring, and who has his worst OPS in 14 years. Add an inconsistent Mookie Betts and an incredibly streaky Teoscar Hernández to an already-shaky lineup.
It’s been such an unsteady year, Andrew Friedman’s two big offseason acquisitions have been busts. Edwin Díaz has been terrible, and then injured, then terrible again. Kyle Tucker has been terrible, then worse, then mostly invisible.
Even the Dodgers two role-playing heroes have seemingly disappeared. Kiké Hernández, at age 35, has his lowest home-run total — three — in 12 years. Miguel Rojas, at age 37, has his lowest home run and RBI totals in nine years.
The Dodgers clinch a playoff berth with their 4-1 victory over the Cincinnati Reds, reaching the postseason for a record-tying 14th consecutive year.
As if they didn’t have enough problems on the field and at the plate, check out the mound. No, don’t.
Even what should be their strength is now being threatened. Blake Snell left Wednesday’s game early with groin issues and Tyler Glasnow recently complained of general discomfort. This leaves a proven playoff rotation of two, Yoshinobu Yamamoto and Tarik Skubal, and if you think Yamamoto threw a lot of innings last October, this time he won’t be able to leave the mound for a month.
In all, this is a Dodger team facing its toughest challenge yet, their quest for an historic three-peat much tougher than the last two journeys, one that will require arguably the greatest stretch of baseball in franchise history to complete.
This division title is a nice beginning.
It could also be the end.
